34.title: Chair Kilmer Urges House to Adopt Committee Recommendations for 117th Congress
34.description: Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress (“Select Committee”) Chair Derek Kilmer (D-WA) testified today before the U.S. House Committee on Rules about the recommendations the Select Committee has made to improve House operations. The Rules Committee hosted a Member Day Hearing on Proposed Rules Changes for the 117th Congress. Chair Kilmer shared a number of the recommendations passed by the Select Committee and how these bipartisan ideas to improve the House rules would help build capacity and ultimately strengthen Congress. Last week, the Select Committee passed its final round of recommendations, bringing the total passed during the 116th Congress to 97.

Members the Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress (“Select Committee”) hosted a discussion with members of the American Political Science Association (APSA) to discuss ongoing recommendations for congressional reform, with a specific focus on congressional capacity, the need for a diverse congressional staff, and the congressional schedule and calendar.
 
Dr. Eric Schickler, Professor of Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley and co-chair of the APSA Task Force on Congressional Reform, Dr. Ruth Bloch Rubin, Assistant Professor in the Department of Political Science at the University of Chicago and member of the Congressional Capacity Subcommittee on the APSA Task Force, and Dr. Michael D. Minta, Associate Professor in Political Science at the University of Minnesota, Twin Cities joined the Members to share their findings from the APSA Task Force, their research on congressional capacity, operations and staffing, and the recommendations their Task Force have drafted.

40.title: The Select Committee on the Modernization of Congress: Conversation on Congressional Staffing
40.description:
Chair Kilmer: 

Let’s go ahead and get started.

Welcome to the Modernization Committee’s virtual discussion on compensation, recruitment, and retention of congressional staff.
Before moving to the topic at hand, I’d like to quickly acknowledge the difficult events of the past week. I know that we’re all dealing with a lot of emotions … and that it’s hard to focus on the particulars of committee work when the painful reality of what’s happening across the country is right before us. So I just want to say that I really appreciate your presence here today and I hope everyone is doing okay.

One year ago, this committee met to discuss staff recruitment and retention issues and to consider a very broad range of reforms. The idea was to put everything on the table and begin an early conversation about the biggest problems and the best solutions. I think we all knew that staffing would be one of the most challenging issues in our mandate; but we also knew it was – without a doubt – one of the most consequential.

Staff are the backbone of this institution. They are dedicated public servants who are here because they want to do meaningful work.  They choose careers on the Hill despite the long hours, the lack of job security, and lower pay compared to what they could make in the executive branch and private sector. 

Congress is fortunate to attract such talented and hard-working staff. The challenge is keeping them here. We know that turnover rates for House staff are really high and while there’s churn between Hill offices, the typical staffer leaves the Hill after 4 or 5 years. That’s right about the time they’ve picked up a lot of institutional knowledge and policy expertise.

As unfortunate as this pattern is, it makes sense. For a lot of staffers, the desire to serve the public is eventually outweighed by the need for a better work/life balance, and the need to make more money to afford housing, support families, and put kids through college. This reality puts Congress at a disadvantage compared to the executive branch and the private sector. 

The bottom line is this: until Congress can offer competitive pay and benefits, Congress will continue to lose talented and smart staff. And rather than view them as replaceable, we should create an environment that encourages the best staffers to stay.  

I’m looking forward to this discussion today and to hearing what our experts recommend.

Before turning it over to Vice Chair Graves, let me just say that this virtual discussion will run much like the others. 

After the Vice Chair finishes his remarks, I’ll introduce our experts and give them 5 minutes each to share some thoughts. 
Then we’ll move to questions and members will have 5 minutes each. 

I’d like to now invite Tom to share his thoughts.

Vice Chair Graves:

Thank you Mr. Chairman, and thank you for continuing to hold these important conversations as we continue working virtually for the American people. 
 
Last June we explored this topic a bit, and highlighted the need for the People’s House to truly reflect the people that we serve. 
 
It’s important we attract and retain a workforce comprised of different voices, backgrounds and skills. 
 
The recommendations we made last July were the first step towards modernizing our human resources capabilities here in the House.
 
There’s more work to do when it comes to supporting the men and women who help us draft legislation and serve as the first line of communication with our constituents. 
 
I’m looking forward to hearing more from our experts today, who have spent a lot of time examining congressional staff data and trends. 
 
We are eager to continue making recommendations for the whole House and I appreciate the opportunity to continue this important conversation.

Experts:

We’re joined today by two experts who have a lot of experience working on congressional staffing issues. 

Casey Burgat, Director of the Legislative Affairs at the Graduate School of Political Management at George Washington University and Kathryn Pearson, Associate Professor at the University of Minnesota, specializing in American Politics; her research focuses on the United States Congress, congressional elections, political parties, and women and politics.
